newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers return to road blocks.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers return to road blocks.

text.p: Greek farmers resumed a road blockade that has paralysed the country for over three weeks after a meeting with the government over their demands for cheaper fuel and subsidies ended in deadlock.
"We return to where we came from. The barricades. The government said "no' to our just demands and our struggle continues and will intensify," Vangelis Boutas, a farmer's union leader, said.
About 7,000 farmers from central Greece travelled to Athens in coaches on Thursday and held a rally outside the Greek parliament to press their demands.
They want lower fuel prices, higher price supports and $1.3 billion in debts rescheduled.
A farmer's committee met Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas, who reiterated that there was no money to satisfy their demands.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis has refused to meet the farmers, saying they must first abandon the blockade that has cut Greece in half, crippling commerce and transport.
The rally took place during a parliamentary debate on the 1997 austerity budget, which imposes new taxes and abolishes dozens of tax breaks, prompting a wave of strikes in recent weeks.
The farmers have blocked roads with tractors, causing transport chaos and inflicting more than $100 million dmage to the economy, according to official figures.

The farmers ended a number of smaller barricades in the past six days but kept intact three big blocks on the main north-south highway linking Athens with the northern port of Salonika, Greece's second largest city.
"We will return to the smaller blocks as well. Mr Simitis will find us on the roads over Christmas, next year, and until next Easter if needed," Achilleas Gatsiakos, a cotton grower, said.
Transport was also being hit by a seamen's strike against Simitis' tight incomes policy.
The seamen called a new 24-hour strike for Friday after stopping many ships from docking on Thursday and clashing with police at several ports
The Panhellenic Seamen's Federation (PNO) said it had extended the strike, which began on Monday, to protest against rising unemployment and the abolition of special tax exemptions.
Police said there were clashes at the ports of Piraeus, near Athens, and Patras in western Greece.
Simitis has stood firm against workers' demands, saying a tight budget was the only way to secure Greece's prospects of joining the European Monetary Union in the next five years.
In an interview published on Thursday in Nitro magazine, Simitis stood by his rejection of concessions for farmers or other workers who have staged protests.

"I'd rather go home (quit)," he said when asked if he would yield to protesters. "My job is to spread the existing money in a socially just way, and that is why we must fight so as not to succumb to blackmail."
